objectives: Sort animals into plant-eaters, meat-eaters and mixed-eaters.
Name the parts of an animal that show what it eats.
Describe the diet of a familiar animal.
Explain why animals need water as well as food.
Use the new words for diets and for eating.
Watch an animal feed and describe what it eats.

sections.body:
Food is the fuel of an animal's body. Animals eat so they can move, think, grow, and stay warm.

But where does all that food come from? Almost every bite starts with the **sun**. Plants use sunlight to make sugar inside their leaves. That sugar is the plant's food, made from air and water.

Then an animal eats the plant, or eats an animal that ate the plant. The energy passes along, from sun to grass to cow to child. Almost all the energy in your body travelled up that chain.

That is why plants matter so much. Remove the plants and the animals lose their food, and then people lose theirs too.

Every animal has its own **diet**, the foods it eats. A diet is not just what an animal likes. It is what its body can digest and what it must have to stay alive.

An animal that eats the wrong food can become ill. An animal that eats too much of the wrong food can get very heavy. And an animal that cannot find enough of its own food has to travel further, or move house, or starve.

So the first question about any animal is a simple one: what is on its table?
examples: The energy in my body came from the sun.
A cow's diet is grass, and that grass makes our milk.
Every animal has its own diet.
sections.heading: Why animals need food, and where it comes from

sections.body:
Scientists sort animals into three big groups by what they eat.

**Herbivores** are plant-eaters. Their teeth are flat and wide, good for grinding grass and leaves. Cows, goats, horses, elephants, rabbits and many insects are herbivores. A cow eats grass for hours, and its stomach is divided into parts so it can digest grass well.

**Carnivores** are meat-eaters. Their teeth are sharp and pointed, good for cutting and tearing. Lions, tigers, wolves, eagles, sharks and crocodiles are carnivores. A carnivore often has strong jaws and very sharp eyesight, because hunting is hard work.

**Omnivores** eat both plants and animals. Humans are omnivores. So are bears, pigs, rats, crows and dogs. A bear eats berries in summer and fish when the salmon come.

Some animals change their diet with the season, and those are called **seasonal eaters**. In spring a bear eats mostly plants. In autumn it fills up on nuts to last through winter.

And a few animals are **scavengers**. They eat what others have left, like the vulture, the hyena and many insects. Cleaned-up food is food too, and it stops the ground from filling up with dead things.
examples: A cow is a herbivore, so it has flat teeth.
A tiger has sharp teeth for tearing meat.
A bear is an omnivore, so it eats berries and fish.
sections.heading: Three kinds of eaters

sections.body:
These are the words that let you talk about what an animal eats.

A **diet** is the set of foods an animal eats. One animal can have a different diet in summer and in winter.

A **herbivore** is an animal that eats plants. A **carnivore** eats other animals. An **omnivore** eats both.

**Energy** is the power a body gets from food. Every movement you make uses some of it.

A **predator** hunts and eats other animals. The animal being hunted is the **prey**. Sometimes the same animal is the predator today and the prey tomorrow.

**Digestion** is the slow work of breaking food down so the body can use it. It starts in the mouth and goes on inside the stomach and the intestines.

**Hibernation** is the deep sleep some animals do through the cold months. They eat a lot in autumn, sleep all winter, and wake up hungry in spring.
sections.heading: The words about eating, one by one

terms.example: A bear's diet is berries, nuts and sometimes fish.
terms.gloss: The set of foods an animal eats. The diet can change with the season.

terms.example: The rabbit is a herbivore and it eats grass.
terms.gloss: An animal that eats plants, such as a cow, a goat or a rabbit.

terms.example: The shark is a carnivore with very sharp teeth.
terms.gloss: An animal that eats other animals, such as a lion, a shark or a tiger.

terms.example: We are omnivores, so we eat rice and fish.
terms.gloss: An animal that eats both plants and animals, such as a bear, a pig or a person.

terms.example: The fox is the predator and the mouse is the prey.
terms.gloss: A predator hunts and eats other animals. The animal being hunted is the prey.

sections.body:
Different animals solve the same problem in different ways.

**Teeth tell the story.** A carnivore has pointed teeth for tearing and flat teeth for crushing bone. A herbivore has broad flat teeth for grinding leaves. A bird that cracks seeds has a strong beak. A bird that drinks nectar has a thin tube beak. A snake has teeth that hold on but cannot chew, so it swallows its food whole.

**Beaks and bills are tools too.** The eagle's hooked beak tears meat. The duck's flat bill strains tiny plants out of water. The woodpecker's long beak reaches insects deep inside a tree.

**Some animals eat and store.** A squirrel hides nuts for winter. A honey bee stores honey in the hive. A camel keeps fat in its hump and uses it when food is short.

**Animals chew in different ways.** A cow chews, swallows, and chews again later. A bird usually swallows food whole. Many animals eat slowly because their food is hard.

**Plants are not only food.** A bird uses twigs and grass to build a nest. A rabbit uses its teeth to gnaw. A giraffe uses a long tongue to reach the highest leaves, where no other animal can go.

Watch an animal feed and you can learn its whole body plan from one small meal.
examples: Its sharp teeth are for tearing meat.
The duck's flat bill strains plants out of the water.
The giraffe's long tongue reaches the top leaves.
sections.heading: How animals find, eat and use their food

sections.body:
You do not need to be an expert. A few good clues will tell you what an animal eats, and you can watch and check.

Look at the teeth or the beak first. Pointed means meat. Flat and wide means plants. A long, thin bill usually means fish or insects.

Look at the eyes and the body. Animals that hunt usually have sharp eyes and lean bodies. Animals that graze usually have wide eyes and big bodies.

Watch where the animal goes. A cow stands in grass and eats it. A swallow dips over water. A woodpecker knocks on a tree.

Look at the droppings. Seed-eaters leave round, grainy ones. Meat-eaters leave darker, shiny ones.

And look at who is afraid of it. The animal that hunts is the predator. The one that runs away is the prey.

If you are not sure, write down what you saw and keep watching. The answer almost always shows up at feeding time.
examples: Its flat teeth tell me it eats plants.
The swallow dips over the water to catch insects.
I will watch it again at feeding time.
sections.heading: How to work out what an animal eats
steps: Look at the teeth or the beak.
Look at the eyes and the shape of the body.
Watch where the animal goes to feed.
Look at what it leaves behind.
Watch who runs away from it.
Write down what you saw and check again.

sections.body:
Food is not only about animals. Plants need animals just as much.

Bees, butterflies, flies and beetles carry pollen between flowers. Without them, many plants cannot make seeds, and our food gets harder to grow.

Animals spread seeds. A bear eats berries and drops the seeds far away. A bird carries a seed in its beak and forgets where it dropped it. Even dung beetles move seeds from one place to another.

Animals also make the soil good. Their droppings feed the tiny living things in the earth, and those living things make the soil that plants grow in.

And every animal needs water, not only food. Water carries nutrients and oxygen through the body and helps an animal stay cool. A camel can go days without a drink, but even it cannot live without water forever.

So the next time you eat your dinner, remember the long chain behind it: the sun, the plant, the animal, and you.
examples: The bee carries pollen so the tree can make fruit.
The bird drops the seed far from the tree.
Even a camel cannot live without water forever.
sections.heading: Why plants and animals need each other

item.summary: Every animal has its own table, and its table decides where it lives and what it does. After reading this, you can sort animals into plant-eaters, meat-eaters and mixed-eaters, watch for the signs that tell you what an animal eats, and explain why plants and animals depend on each other.
item.title: What Do Animals Eat?
